name: Doorway pec stretch

lead: The doorway pec stretch lengthens the muscles at the front of the chest by leaning through a door frame with the forearm braced on it. It needs no equipment and takes under a minute.
People use it to loosen a tight chest and help the shoulders sit back, which can make posture look more open and the upper body more upright.

paras: The arm is fixed against the frame so that stepping forward pulls the pectoral muscle and front shoulder into a lengthened position. Lifters usually pair it with upper-back exercises.

Over-stretching the front of the shoulder can cause discomfort, and people with shoulder instability or prior labrum surgery are often cautious about how far they go. Product-free and low risk otherwise.

chain: Shoulders can settle back and open
angle.text: People use the stretch to counter a hunched, rounded-shoulder look, aiming for an open chest and squarer shoulders. It is commonly paired with upper-back work such as rows and face pulls.

lead: The doorway pec stretch is a simple chest-opening stretch: the forearm or hand rests on a door frame and the body leans or steps forward, lengthening the pectoral muscles at the front of the chest. People use it to loosen a tight chest and ease the rounded-shoulder look, so the shoulders sit more open and the chest appears broader and more upright.

The pectoralis major is a fan-shaped muscle that flexes, adducts and internally rotates the upper arm and draws the shoulder blade forward and down [1]. General descriptions of posture note that tight pectoral muscles together with weaker upper-back and abdominal muscles can affect how a person stands [2]. Lifters in training logs on T Nation mention pec stretches as part of warm-ups and mobility sessions alongside face pulls, hangs and hip-flexor work [3][4].

Stretching research distinguishes static from dynamic methods: static and PNF stretching increase range of motion more than dynamic or ballistic stretching, and holds of 60 seconds or more before exercise can temporarily reduce strength [5]. The doorway stretch is a static, passive stretch of the front of the chest and shoulder. No published trial has tested it for changing how the shoulders look.

paras: The usual form places a forearm vertically on a door frame with the elbow near shoulder height, then a step forward through the doorway turns the chest away from the arm. Variations change the arm height to emphasise different parts of the chest, and some people use a wall, a corner, a rack or a resistance band instead [6]. Lifters also describe weighted and ring-based pec stretches in their logs [4].

The pectoralis major covers the upper chest and acts on the humerus [1]. Beneath it lies the pectoralis minor, a thin triangular muscle arising from ribs 3 to 5 and inserting on the coracoid process of the scapula; it stabilises the scapula against the chest wall and moves it down and forward, and its tendon crosses beneath structures entering the arm [7]. Because the doorway stretch loads the front of the shoulder joint and both pectoral muscles at once, people use the height of the forearm on the frame to change which part of the chest feels the pull [6].

Tightness in the chest is one part of what physical therapy sources describe as a hunched upper-body pattern. Wikipedia's description of forward head posture lists a rounded upper back with the head carried in front of the shoulder line, shortened muscles at the back of the neck, and weak or lengthened mid-back muscles and deep neck flexors [8]. Its suggested minimum combination of care is strengthening the mid and lower back, shoulder-blade retractors and deep neck flexors, stretching the muscles that pull the head forward, and mobilising the thoracic spine [8].

sections.h: Posture, appearance and the open-chest idea
paras: The look people want from the stretch is shoulders that sit back and down over a more upright rib cage, so the chest appears broader and the neck sits less forward. The rationale is a muscle-balance one: stretch the pulling-forward muscles at the front, strengthen the retracting muscles at the back. A 2019 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found a correlation between forward head posture and neck pain in adults but not adolescents, and a 2014 study estimated that hunching increases load on the neck compared with erect posture [8]. These findings concern comfort and load rather than looks.

Stretching literature suggests that regular stretching increases stretch tolerance, probably through changes in how discomfort is perceived, and may also change tissue stiffness and muscle geometry, though the roles of these mechanisms are not well understood [5]. Static stretching does not appear to reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness [5].

In appearance-focused communities the stretch sits in the posture toolkit: loosen the chest, strengthen the upper back, and the shoulders look more open. Training-log posts show it used as a warm-up between sets and on mobility days, and some lifters write that a good pec stretch gives them a pump in the shoulders [3][6]. Others use it after returning from shoulder injury to regain overhead range [9]. Discussion of long-muscle-length training also appears, where lifters note that working in a stretched position is linked to muscle growth [10].

Training logs show variants: one lifter returning from labrum repair surgery notes doing mobility work and trying to get the pecs stretched out [9], another lists rings upside-down to front hold with pec stretch, face pulls, dead hangs and weighted pec stretch as part of a 30-minute morning stretching session [4], and a third uses a band to stretch lat, pec and biceps before upper-body sessions [6]. A separate poster described a pec stretch as the best he had had so far, and reported a good shoulder pump afterward [3].

No studies found on the doorway pec stretch itself. Wider research on stretching covers range of motion, performance and injury; reviews cited by Wikipedia report that static and PNF stretching improve range of motion more than dynamic stretching, that long static holds before exercise can temporarily reduce strength, and that evidence that stretching alone prevents injury is debated [5]. Studies of forward head posture concern neck pain and are not specific to chest stretching [8].

lore.intro: The stretch comes up in lifting forums as routine mobility work rather than a headline technique [3][6].
